summary: Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed an interactive "Sky Time Machine" web application using Next.js 16, React 19, and Tailwind 4 that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey into an accessible citizen-science workbench. Because raw astronomical FITS files and multi-epoch spectral datasets are typically locked behind complex command-line software, we solved this barrier by building a resilient, SSRF-safe backend that resolves target coordinates via SIMBAD, fetches IRSA archives using opaque allowlisted record IDs and Promise.any collection fallbacks, and streams parsed scalar pixels alongside Gaia DR3 star catalogs directly to the browser. On the client side, hand-written, zero-dependency TypeScript image math powers real-time percentile stretches, synchronized blink comparators, reveal sliders, pixel-level difference metrics, a wavelength-band selector, and real 3-band false-color RGB composites on an HTML5 canvas—all while keeping underlying data unmutated and clearly framing anomalies as exploratory clues rather than formal discoveries. By combining beginner-friendly tours with shareable comparison links, our platform empowers students, educators, and space enthusiasts to hunt for moving asteroids and variable stars, with future plans to integrate known-object ephemeris cross-matching and archival multi-mission overlays.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Our web application transforms NASA’s SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey into an interactive "Sky Time Machine" for exploring how the cosmos changes over time. Users can search any celestial object or sky coordinate, inspect multi-epoch infrared observations, and compare two snapshots side-by-side using synchronized blink comparators, draggable reveal sliders, and pixel-level difference maps. Users can also isolate specific spectra via a wavelength-band selector or blend three bands into a real false-color RGB composite to reveal thermal and structural variations. Under the hood, a server-side proxy resolves coordinates through CDS Sesame/SIMBAD and fetches FITS files and Gaia DR3 star catalogs from NASA/IPAC IRSA archives, streaming raw scalar pixels to the browser for real-time rendering on an HTML5 canvas.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Our platform removes that barrier, offering instant browser-based visualization, sharRaw astronomical FITS files and multi-epoch spectral datasets normally require specialized desktop software and steep technical expertise. eable comparison links, and a 4-step beginner tour that teaches core infrared astronomy concepts. The intended impact is to democratize space science—empowering students, educators, and curious citizens to actively hunt for transient clues like moving asteroids or variable stars while building genuine scientific literacy.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

We built the entire stack using Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS 4, keeping the footprint lightweight with zero heavy external imaging libraries. Aside from fitsjs for server-side FITS parsing, all astronomical image math—including percentile windowing (P1–P99.5), asinh/log/sqrt stretches, 3-band RGB compositing, Gaia star hit-testing, pixel-difference metrics, and non-destructive clarity enhancements—was hand-written from scratch in TypeScript. Data is sourced via NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA v2 and Gator APIs) and CDS Sesame/SIMBAD.

Creativity & Key Design Factors

Rather than building a static image gallery, we creatively reimagined multi-epoch astronomy as an intuitive time-travel workbench complete with custom cosmic motion graphics, interactive blink/difference comparators, and non-destructive before/after enhancement sliders. Throughout development, our team prioritized three critical factors:

  • Scientific Integrity: Raw scalar data is never mutated, every visualization is clearly labeled, and detected anomalies are framed honestly as "candidate clues" requiring follow-up rather than formal discoveries.
  • Security: An SSRF-safe architecture hides raw archive URLs behind opaque base64url record IDs validated against strict server allowlists.
  • Resilience: Automated Promise.any collection fallbacks, 5-minute caching, retry logic, and demo-data fallbacks ensure a smooth user experience even if upstream archives experience latency.
  • User-Friendliness & Accessibility: Designed for non-specialists with instant name autocomplete, curated featured targets, a 4-step interactive beginner tour, and responsive controls so anyone can explore deep-space infrared data without prior astronomy experience.
